#### One theme, six doors: which call should host which idea

All six screens arrived at the same intersection: **AI data center siting and water under compound flash drought and heat extremes**. Every screen also found that this intersection is unoccupied in funded work. No NSF award titled on "data center siting" turned up in the Award API ([NSF API query](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json?keyword=%22data%20center%20siting%22)). Every data center CAREER award found is about operations: power flexibility, thermal management and carbon ([NSF 2541996](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2541996), [NSF 2544321](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2544321), [NSF 2340042](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2340042)). The DOE-funded data center energy-water work at PNNL uses state or HUC2 scale through GCAM-USA, without Earth-system drought extremes ([OSTI 2998851](https://www.osti.gov/dataexplorer/biblio/dataset/2998851), [OSTI 2584365](https://www.osti.gov/dataexplorer/biblio/dataset/2584365)). The opening is real. The danger is that one good project sent to every door becomes a duplicate-submission problem.

**NSF duplicate-submission risk.** NSF returns without review a proposal that duplicates, or is substantially similar to, one already under review from the same submitter ([NSF PAPPG](https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg); the section was not reopened in this research, so confirm the current wording). The EWRE, CMMI-EBE and CAREER screens each picked nearly the same project as their lead: robust siting and design of data centers under heat-drought uncertainty, with withdrawal and thermal-discharge constraints. Those three cannot be pending at once. EWRE's own page warns that "buildings and cities" belong in CMMI ([EWRE program page](https://www.nsf.gov/funding/opportunities/energy-water-resource-engineering)), so the same proposal could even be moved between the two programs.

The partition below keeps one theme across six proposals while giving each a distinct question, decision variable and method:

| Host call | Idea | Distinct question | What it must NOT contain |
|---|---|---|---|
| USGS 104g (2026-11-12) | U1 + U2 (with U3, U4 as data layers) | How much water do Tennessee data centers use now, and how will that change seasonally and under extremes? (observation, estimation, validation) | Siting optimization as a deliverable; SMR thermal discharge (104b scope) |
| DOE BER (before 2027-04-01) | B1 | How predictable is sub-basin water availability for energy loads under compound extremes? (Earth-system science) | Optimization as the headline; boreal ecology |
| NSF GEO Core (rolling) | G1 (+ G2, G3 as aims) | What controls ecosystem ET and carbon recovery after flash drought? (no data centers) | Decision support; FFAR tool deliverables |
| NSF CBET EWRE (rolling, early 2027) | E1 (+ E3, E2 module) | Which cooling technology, water source and operating policy should a facility use under drought-heat uncertainty? Candidate sites are fixed inputs. | Regional siting and capacity expansion (reserved for CAREER) |
| NSF CMMI AMDO (rolling) | C1 (+ C3) | How do you site when rules (moratoria, tariffs, queues) respond to your own siting? (optimization methodology) | Hydro-climate hazard modeling as the core |
| NSF CAREER (2027-07-28) | K1 | Regional, multi-decade siting and capacity planning under spatially correlated compound extremes, with an education plan | Facility cooling co-design (EWRE); policy endogeneity theory (AMDO) |

Under this plan, CMMI-EBE idea C2 is held back. If the PI turns out to be ineligible for CAREER (see the CAREER section), or if program officers prefer EBE over a CAREER, C2 becomes the vehicle for K1's research and K1 is not submitted. Cross-agency submissions (DOE and NSF, USGS and NSF) are allowed, but each must list the others in Current and Pending Support, and the 104g program explicitly screens for "potential overlap or duplication between the proposed project and any other funded or proposed project" ([104g NOFO](https://files.simpler.grants.gov/opportunities/2c5fcf26-2264-42ae-9bc9-60f591fd770c/attachments/1931b7a5-8a2e-4007-a158-cbf31be312cd/Foa_Content_of_G27AS00164_100226.pdf)).

**Overlap with the lab's own grants.** Two funded projects sit at the center of this theme. The USGS 104b project, "Decision Support for TDEC to Reduce Freshwater Withdrawals and Thermal Discharges from Data Centers and Small Modular Reactors in Tennessee" ($84K, 1 year from 2027-01, PI), is closest to any idea centered on SMR thermal discharge or TDEC decision tools. That is why U5 is dropped and E2 is only a module. The UT ISSE project, "The Local Footprint of AI Data Centers: Noise, Water, and Land-Market Tradeoffs in Tennessee" ($60K, 1 year from 2026-08, PI), is closest to observatory or footprint ideas. That is why K4 is dropped, and it is the data source behind C1's acceptance-hazard model. Every new proposal should present these two grants as preliminary results, data access and a stakeholder link, with one sentence stating what the new proposal does that they do not. The FFAR flash-drought decision-support project (Co-PI) plays the same role for GEO and CAREER-K3, and the DOE/ORNL vulnerability grant (PI) for BER.

##### Ideas: USDA NIFA AFRI A1712 Rapid Response to Weather Events

**Key call rules and the qualifying event.** A1712 funds only **Extension or Integrated** projects (Standard or FASE grants), **12 months, at most $300,000 including indirect costs**. An application "must be submitted within 45 calendar days after a weather event or disaster", must "directly address effects associated with a recent weather event", and must include a statement on timing and relevance when the event is prolonged. One or more deliverables must be implemented **within 90 days of award**, the narrative is limited to **7 pages**, adoption potential must be measurable, and the program "limits applications to **one per PD per funding cycle**". Work with a preparedness, recovery, or mitigation focus is pointed to **A1701 CARE** instead. A mentoring plan is required for all FY2026 AFRI applications. After submitting, notify afri-rapidresponse@usda.gov ([NOFO MOD6, section 7g, Table 39](https://files.simpler.grants.gov/opportunities/10a7404c-3e2f-4355-9044-78c8bafc35cd/attachments/1d6366ca-2e3e-48a8-bea7-8303cbbd5500/FY26-AFRI-FAS-NOFO-P-MOD6.pdf)).

The qualifying event is the **2026 Tennessee fall flash drought**. Statewide, D1+ rose from **0.91% (2026-08-25) to 64.22% (2026-10-20)**. On the 2026-10-20 map D2+ is 48.15%, D3+ 18.80%, and the first **D4 (1.16%)** appeared ([USDM TN statistics](https://usdmdataservices.unl.edu/api/StateStatistics/GetDroughtSeverityStatisticsByAreaPercent?aoi=47&startdate=8/1/2026&enddate=10/25/2026&statisticsType=1)). The worst area is **West Tennessee**: D4 covers 64.15% of Lauderdale and 34.31% of Tipton County, D3 covers all of Chester, Fayette, and Hardeman, and 27 counties have some D3. Southern Middle Tennessee is also affected: Lincoln, Giles, Lawrence, Coffee, and Moore are 100% D2, and Marshall (35.69%) and Maury (27.45%) have D3. East Tennessee is largely outside the drought ([USDM TN county statistics](https://usdmdataservices.unl.edu/api/CountyStatistics/GetDroughtSeverityStatisticsByAreaPercent?aoi=TN&startdate=10/20/2026&enddate=10/20/2026&statisticsType=1); [NWS Huntsville statement, valid 2026-09-29](https://www.weather.gov/media/hun/DGT/DGT_HUN_10012026.pdf)). The same year already had a statewide spring drought (about 72% D2 and 27% D3 in May) that cut spring pasture growth ([UT Beef Live.Stock Companion, May 2026](https://utbeef.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/127/2026/05/Live.Stock-Companion-Volume-30-May-2026.pdf)), so forage-livestock producers are hit twice before winter feeding.

**Recommended timing:** anchor the event on the 2026-09-29 USDM map (D2+ jumped to 33.75%, D3 first confirmed by NWS) and **submit by 2026-11-13** (9/29 + 45 days). The first D4 on 2026-10-20 gives a fallback anchor of 2026-12-04; the Grants.gov listing closes 2026-12-31. ###### R1. Flash drought forage and stock-water rapid response for Middle and West Tennessee cattle producers — Pursue (conditional on an extension Co-PD)

###### R2. Did grazing and soil-health practices limit 2026 flash drought damage? ET-based efficacy assessment and extension guidance — Revise (Objective 2 of R1)

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao. **Needed, unconfirmed:** a UT soil-health or cover-crop extension specialist and NRCS Tennessee practice data.

**Approach.** Compare pastures and fields with and without management practices (stockpiled or rotational grazing; cover crops and no-till for crop fields) using satellite ET, water-use efficiency, and greenness drawdown and recovery, with the PI's flash drought WUE and recovery methods; present results at spring 2027 field days.

**Closest existing work and gap.** Satellite evidence on practice efficacy comes from the Corn Belt and is yield-based: across more than 90,000 fields, 3+ years of cover crops reduced maize yields by 5.5% and soybean yields by 3.5% on average, with larger losses in dry springs (Deines et al., *Global Change Biology* 2023; [PNNL record](https://data.pnnl.gov/group/nodes/publication/33662), [Stanford news](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2022/11/cover-crops-can-lower-yields)). Drought-year benefits are self-reported ([SARE 2012 survey](https://www.sare.org/publications/cover-crop-economics/an-in-depth-look-at-management-situations-where-cover-crops-pay-off-faster/when-soil-moisture-is-at-a-deficit-or-irrigation-is-needed)) and field soil-moisture evidence is mixed ([Practical Farmers of Iowa](https://practicalfarmers.org/research/cover-crop-effect-on-soil-water)). No ET- or recovery-based evidence from a documented flash drought in the humid Southeast was found.

**Why us.** The AFM 2026 flash drought WUE and recovery paper and the *J. Hydrol.* 2023 drought-recovery paper. Earlier unfunded proposals on these topics (SE CASC 2026, PI; AFRI A1102 and A1401 2025, Co-PI; 2023 NIFA ranching soil-health, Co-PI) are reusable text, not assets.

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao with Shi Jin (from Spring 2027). A UAS platform, a Part 107 pilot, and farm access are needed; none is listed in the talent pool.

###### N1. Interpretable SI/ML thresholds for heat-driven cascades in the Tennessee Valley energy-water system — Pursue (lead)

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao (PI; heatwave hydrology, flash drought, soil moisture, data-center water). Shi Jin (from Spring 2027; ML pipeline and data engineering: PyTorch, LSTM, YOLO/EfficientNet, a 350K-record ETL and retrieval pipeline, infrared + LiDAR fusion for substation monitoring). Yifan Gao (geospatial analysis, load-growth scenarios). Mingzhou Jin (UT ISE/ISSE, listed collaborator; possible decision-support advisor, role unconfirmed). **Needed, all unconfirmed:** a power-systems or grid-data co-investigator (none in the talent pool); a NOAA collaborator (e.g., an NWS forecast office serving Tennessee or the Southeast Regional Climate Center); a NIHHIS partner-agency contact; a TDEC letter of support (TDEC is named in the 104b grant title, but no letter is documented); TVA or utility data access; optionally a heat-health partner. The ORNL RiTHyMs and UT ReForM river-temperature groups would be natural data partners; they are not in the talent pool.

**Research question and approach.** At what combinations of air temperature, soil-moisture/flash-drought state, river temperature, and electric load do heat impacts begin to cascade (thermoelectric derates and curtailments → load peaks and outages → water-supply stress)? How well does NOAA heat information signal these thresholds in advance, and how does projected data-center load growth shift them? Interpretable ML (gradient boosting with SHAP; monotone or threshold-detecting models) learns joint thresholds for three outcomes, benchmarked against logistic and segmented regression. Inputs: NOAA nClimGrid, URMA/RTMA and NWS heat products; satellite soil moisture; USGS stream temperature; EIA-923/860 plant data; EIA/DOE outage records. Existing river-temperature forecasts (RiTHyMs or ReForM outputs) or simple physics enter as inputs rather than being rebuilt. Deliverables: a public SI/ML-ready threshold dataset, a NOAA Learning Journeys notebook, and threshold briefings co-produced with TDEC and the NIHHIS partner. To keep hazards to people visible, include thresholds at which heat-driven outages cut off cooling for residents.

**Closest existing projects and papers, and the gap.**
- River-temperature ML for TVA exists: ORNL's RiTHyMs, an LSTM model (about 1.1 °C mean absolute error) being applied to TVA-managed rivers ([ORNL news](https://www.ornl.gov/news/ai-model-delivers-river-temperature-insights-strengthening-us-energy-security); [HPCwire 2026-01-15](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/2026/01/15/ornls-sean-turner-on-using-ai-to-bridge-river-models-power-grid-operations/)), and UT Knoxville's hybrid ReForM forecast for TVA ([UT CEE](https://cee.utk.edu/tce-group-develops-novel-forecasting-model-to-predict-river-temperature/)). Both known only from search snippets (bot check on the pages); scope unverified.

###### N2. Compound heat and flash-drought thresholds for Southeastern agriculture and rural water supply — Revise (module of N1)

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao, Yifan Gao (geospatial). Needed, unconfirmed: an agricultural or extension partner, crop/livestock outcome data, small-water-system data.

**Approach.** Apply N1's threshold engine to a second sector: at what soil-moisture-conditioned heat levels do humid Southeastern crops and small water systems cross into loss, using NOAA heat products?

**Closest existing work and gap.** Flash-drought AI is already funded: NSF 2616278/2616279 (UCLA and Ohio State, from 2026-08-15; $502,520 + $390,000), an interpretable multi-task deep-learning flash-drought predictor using soil moisture and heat ([NSF API 2616278](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards/2616278.json?printFields=id,title,abstractText)); also EAGER 2435046, CAREER 2144293 (Auburn), 2414601, 2303457/2303458, and 2406295/2445027 ([NSF API "flash drought"](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json?keyword=%22flash%20drought%22)). Compound heat-drought events outweigh single events for maize yield (Bogenreuther et al. 2025; region not verified) ([PDF](https://epub.uni-bayreuth.de/8863/1/1-s2.0-S0168192325004551-main.pdf)); a Carolinas/Georgia random-forest study linked drought, not heat, to yields ([EGU24-2908](https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU24/EGU24-2908.html)). The remaining gap is narrow: soil-moisture-conditioned heat-impact thresholds for humid Southeastern agriculture and rural water built from NOAA heat information.

**Why us.** PI is Co-PI on the FFAR grant "A multi-source remote sensing-based framework and decision-support tool for flash droughts and floods under climate change" ($434,038, from 04/2024); flash-drought and ET papers ([AFM 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2025.110982); [AFM 2019 BMA](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2019.107759)); ongoing Xi–Hao–Leib–M. Jin irrigation paper under flash drought.

**Risks.** Overlaps the FFAR grant, R1/R5 in [2026-10-25.md](#carried-over-scan-2026-10-25), and K3 in [2026-10-21.md](#carried-over-scan-2026-10-21); no agricultural outcome data or partner confirmed.

**Verdict: Revise.** Fold into N1 as the agriculture and rural-water module (PA3a names "health, built infrastructure, and agriculture"). Do not submit separately.

###### N3. Forecasts of opportunity for U.S. extreme heat preconditioned by soil-moisture deficits — Revise (aim of N1, or standalone only with an S2S co-PI)

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao, Shi Jin. Needed, unconfirmed: an S2S or ML-forecasting co-PI and a NOAA PSL, CPC, or GFDL collaborator.

**Approach.** Interpretable ML identifies windows when soil-moisture and flash-drought states make U.S. (Southeast and Central) heat predictable at weeks 2–4, then tests whether NOAA systems (GEFS, CFSv2, SPEAR seasonal) capture them, as PA3b requires.

**Closest existing work and gap.** Only three NSF awards mention "forecasts of opportunity" ([NSF API](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json?keyword=%22forecasts%20of%20opportunity%22)); the closest is 2616256/2616257 on stratosphere-troposphere coupling ([NSF API 2616257](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards/2616257.json?printFields=id,title,abstractText)). NSF 2435262/2435263 studies soil moisture in observed heatwaves as process science, not ML forecasts of opportunity. Published ML forecast-of-opportunity work centers on tropical sources ([NOAA S2S webinar](https://www.weather.gov/media/climateservices/Arcodia-NOAA-S2S-APS-Webinar.pdf); [DOE EESM record](https://eesm.science.energy.gov/publications/assessing-decadal-variability-subseasonal-forecasts-opportunity-using-explainable-ai)) or Europe ([van Straaten et al.](https://publications.pik-potsdam.de/pubman/item/item_28103_1/component/file_28111/28103oa.pdf); [Weirich-Benet et al., WCE 2024](https://doaj.org/article/5d720f87d154453294b912e23d052a58)); soil-moisture and evaporative-demand forecasts of opportunity have been shown for weeks 3–6 ([NSF PAR 10458479](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10458479)). No U.S. study was found that diagnoses soil-moisture-driven heat forecast-of-opportunity windows with ML and verifies them in NOAA systems.

**Why us (partial).** Heatwave, flash-drought, and soil-moisture papers (above) supply the physical interpretation; PI was topic lead of the RUBISCO Soil Moisture Working Group mini-workshops. The talent pool shows no S2S forecasting or verification publications.

**Risks.** Technical-merit credibility; overlap with B3 in [2026-10-21.md](#carried-over-scan-2026-10-21) (E3SM-RRM predictability).

**Verdict: Revise.** Make it a small N1 aim (when do heat plus flash-drought threshold exceedances become predictable at weeks 2–4?). Standalone only with a confirmed S2S/ML co-PI and a NOAA lab collaborator. Keep NOAA systems here and E3SM in B3.

###### N4. How small and mid-size utilities and water systems use SI/ML tools with NOAA heat and drought information (PA2) — Drop

PA2 requires socio-economic methods and strongly encourages NOAA staff collaboration. Large-utility AI adoption is already surveyed (fewer than a quarter of 49 large U.S. drinking-water utilities used AI: [ASCE JWRMD](https://ascelibrary.com/doi/10.1061/JWRMD5.WRENG-5870); [BYU summary](https://cce.byu.edu/how-do-drinking-water-utilities-use-artificial-intelligence)); aiWATERS studied utilities of all sizes ([VTechWorks](https://vtechworks.lib.vt.edu/items/1eb809d6-947b-4e08-b91e-039380737f95)). The talent pool has no social scientist, survey record, or utility partner, so Hao Lab would only be a technical add-on. Keep at most a light stakeholder-interview task inside N1, run with a partner.

###### N5. SI/ML emulator of land and ecosystem drought response for multi-annual prediction (PA1b) — Drop

PA1b asks for emulators of NOAA models such as SPEAR at 2–10 year leads. GFDL and Ai2 lead this area (ACE and ACE2 learn variability from subseasonal to decadal scales: [ACE](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.02074); [ACE2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.11268); [SPEAR](https://aos.princeton.edu/news/spear-next-generation-gfdl-modeling-system-seasonal-multidecadal-prediction-and-projection)). The PI's model experience is E3SM, not SPEAR, and the lab has no emulator or multi-annual prediction publications. It would also duplicate B2 in [2026-10-21.md](#carried-over-scan-2026-10-21).

### Ideas Overview

Ideas for NOAA-OAR-CPO-2027-33392 were screened on 2026-10-31 under the "Funding Idea Rule" in [CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md), against the full NOFO, the NSF Award API, and the literature. Research notes are in [ideas/2026-10-31/](../ideas/2026-10-31/). "Why us" claims were checked against [talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md](../../talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md) and [talent-pool/resources/hao-lab/](../../talent-pool/resources/hao-lab/); web-only facts are marked as external evidence.

#### Which call should host which idea

**This NOAA call hosts exactly one proposal: N1 under PA3a**, with N2 as an agriculture and rural-water module and N3 as a weeks-2–4 predictability aim. CPO's LOI reply is the go/no-go point; if discouraged, the threshold work can move to CMMI-EBE (C2) or the CAREER plan (K1), not to a second NOAA submission.

NOAA's no-duplication rule means N1 must state what it does that each related project does not, and list every pending proposal in Current and Pending Support:

| Related project or idea | Its question | What N1 must not contain |
|---|---|---|
| USGS 104b TDEC grant (PI, funded) | Reducing withdrawals and thermal discharges from data centers and SMRs, as decision support for TDEC | Thermal-discharge or withdrawal decision tools as deliverables; use 104b only as preliminary work, data access, and the TDEC link |
| UT ISSE footprint grant (PI, funded) | Noise, water, and land-market footprint of AI data centers | Facility-level footprint accounting |
| FFAR flash-drought grant (Co-PI, funded) | Remote-sensing flash-drought and flood decision-support tool | A flash-drought monitoring or decision tool; N2 uses heat-impact thresholds only |
| 2026-10-21 U1/U2 (USGS 104g) | Tennessee data-center water use and demand forecasts | Data-center water-use estimates or demand forecasts as deliverables (load growth only as a scenario input) |
| 2026-10-21 B1/B3 (DOE BER) | Earth-system predictability of water availability with E3SM-RRM | E3SM projections; N1/N3 stay observation-driven with NOAA systems |
| 2026-10-21 C2 (CMMI-EBE, hold) and K1 (CAREER) | Resilience and robust siting of the data center-grid-water system under compound extremes | Siting or capacity optimization and system design; N1 produces empirical hazard thresholds those projects could later use |
| 2026-10-21 E1/E2 (CBET-EWRE) | Facility cooling and water-source co-design; SMR thermal discharge | Facility or cooling design |
| 2026-10-21 G1 (GEO Core) and K3 (CAREER backup) | Flash-drought ecosystem recovery; stochastic water allocation | Recovery-process science; allocation optimization |
| 2026-10-25 R1 (A1712) and R5 (A1701) | Forage and stock-water rapid response; irrigation planning | Forage, livestock, or irrigation decision guidance in N2 |

The closest overlap is C2/K1 (same region, hazard, and system). The safe line is method and output: N1 is observational, interpretable-ML hazard science producing a threshold dataset triggered by NOAA heat information; C2 and K1 are design and optimization projects.

#### Open items and limits

- **Before the LOI (2026-11-17), in order:** (1) confirm UT Knoxville's eRA Commons registration and the PI's PD/PI account; (2) identify a NOAA collaborator (e.g., the relevant NWS forecast office or the Southeast Regional Climate Center); (3) identify a NIHHIS partner-agency contact; (4) ask TDEC for a letter of support; (5) decide on a power-systems or grid-data co-investigator (co-authors on the RSER wildfire-grid paper are candidates only); (6) confirm RiTHyMs and ReForM scope. None of these partners is confirmed.
- **Unverified:** cpo.noaa.gov returned 403, so CPO's FY2024–FY2026 MAPP, NIHHIS, and AdSci SI/ML and heat awards were not checked — the main hole in the duplication check. ORNL and UT pages returned a bot check. Current Browns Ferry permit terms and post-2011 TVA derates were not verified. A Tennessee data-center heat-wave news item was not opened ([DCD](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/heat-wave-causes-headache-for-tennessee-data-centers/)). Outage data resolution (OE-417, EAGLE-I) was not checked.
- **Team facts:** every "why us" item appears in the talent-pool files. The talent pool contains no ML-for-prediction or S2S publications; no NOAA, NIHHIS, utility, TVA, or health partner; no letters of support; and no power-systems co-investigator. Shi Jin joins in Spring 2027, before the 2027-09-01 start.
- **Search limits:** funded-project checks relied on the NSF Award API with quoted phrases; NOAA award lists, USAspending, and NIH RePORTER were not searched systematically; several literature items were read as abstracts or snippets. Gap claims mean "not found in the sources checked", not "proven absent".
